quests.instruction: During the tense contract negotiation, the CFO gave no reaction at all to the shockingly low offer, revealing nothing about what he was really thinking.
quests.hint: It's about maintaining a completely neutral expression that reveals nothing about your true thoughts or feelings.
quests.explanation: 'Poker face' describes a neutral expression that reveals nothing about one's true thoughts, especially useful in negotiation. "She kept her poker face on through the entire salary discussion."
quests.origin: From poker, where skilled players hide any reaction to their cards to avoid giving opponents clues about their hand.

quests.instruction: In a heated boardroom negotiation, a skilled executive avoids ___ too early, keeping competitors guessing about the company's real strategy.
quests.hint: It means revealing your true plans or position, usually before it's strategically wise to do so.
quests.explanation: 'Show your cards' means to reveal your true plans or position, often prematurely. "A good negotiator never shows their cards too early."
quests.origin: From card games, where revealing your hand to opponents gives away your strategy and weakens your position.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Use your most powerful advantage or piece of information at the most effective, decisive moment.
quests.explanation: 'Play your trump card' means to use your strongest advantage at the most decisive moment. "She played her trump card by revealing the competing offer during the final round of negotiations."
quests.origin: From card games featuring a 'trump' suit that outranks all others, where playing a trump card guarantees winning that round.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Twenty minutes into a dry, jargon-heavy presentation, the CEO noticed people checking their phones and quietly closing their laptops instead of listening."
quests.hint: It's about a speaker losing an audience's attention and engagement during a presentation or speech.
quests.explanation: 'Lose the room' means to lose an audience's attention or engagement while speaking. "He lost the room the moment he started reading numbers straight off the slides."
quests.origin: A modern extension of 'read the room,' where a speaker fails to keep the collective attention of the group physically present.

quests.instruction: By opening with a personal, vulnerable story instead of statistics, the new speaker managed to ___ within the first two minutes.
quests.hint: It means gaining an audience's favor, trust, or enthusiasm, often unexpectedly.
quests.explanation: 'Win over the crowd' means to gain an audience's favor or enthusiasm. "Her honesty about the failed launch actually won over the skeptical crowd."
quests.origin: A transparent metaphor treating an audience's support as something to be earned, or 'won,' through persuasion or charm.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Try to persuade people who already agree with you, making the persuasion effort unnecessary.
quests.explanation: 'Preach to the choir' means to argue a point to people who already agree with it. "Telling this audience that climate change is real is preaching to the choir."
quests.origin: A literal image of a preacher addressing the church choir, who are already devoted believers and don't need convincing.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Rather than lecturing the team about working late, the new director simply stayed until midnight herself during the crunch period, without saying a word about it."
quests.hint: It's about influencing others' behavior through your own actions rather than instructions or speeches.
quests.explanation: 'Lead by example' means to influence others through your own behavior rather than instruction. "The captain led by example, showing up early to every single practice."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase, contrasting leading through demonstrated action with leading purely through verbal command.

quests.instruction: The CEO's calm, measured response to the crisis in the first company-wide email seemed to ___ for how the entire organization handled the following weeks.
quests.hint: It means establishing the general mood, approach, or standard that others tend to follow afterward.
quests.explanation: 'Set the tone' means to establish the general mood or approach that influences what follows. "Her opening remarks set the tone for a respectful, productive debate."
quests.origin: A musical metaphor, where the opening note or 'tone' of a piece establishes the mood for the rest of the performance.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Actually demonstrate the values or standards you claim to hold, through consistent behavior.
quests.explanation: 'Walk the walk' means to demonstrate your claimed values through consistent action, not just words. "She doesn't just talk about diversity — she walks the walk in her hiring."
quests.origin: Part of the fuller phrase 'talk the talk and walk the walk,' here used independently to emphasize action over speech.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Despite months of small marketing tweaks, sales numbers stayed almost exactly the same — none of it made any meaningful difference at all."
quests.hint: It's about causing a measurable, significant change in results, especially in a business or data context.
quests.explanation: 'Move the needle' means to cause a measurable, meaningful change in results. "None of the small changes actually moved the needle on customer retention."
quests.origin: From a literal measuring dial, or 'needle,' whose visible movement indicates a real, measurable shift in a reading.

quests.instruction: Instead of tackling the complex system redesign first, the team decided to fix the easy, quick wins — the ___ — to build early momentum.
quests.hint: It refers to the easiest tasks or opportunities to accomplish, requiring the least effort for a return.
quests.explanation: 'Low-hanging fruit' describes the easiest tasks or opportunities to accomplish first. "Let's grab the low-hanging fruit before tackling the harder problems."
quests.origin: A literal image from fruit picking, where the fruit closest to the ground is the easiest to reach and harvest first.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "After a full month fixing only small, easy bugs, the team realized the product's deeper, structural problems hadn't been touched at all."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Address only a small, superficial part of a much larger issue, leaving the core problem essentially untouched.
quests.explanation: 'Barely scratch the surface' means to address only a small part of a much larger issue. "Fixing the typos barely scratched the surface of the report's real problems."
quests.origin: A literal image of a light scratch that only marks the very top layer of something, leaving everything beneath untouched.

quests.instruction: A friend excitedly describes an investment opportunity a total stranger pitched to them online, promising guaranteed huge returns. Which idiom fits the healthy suspicion you should feel?
quests.hint: It's about sensing that something is dishonest or wrong, even without concrete proof yet.
quests.explanation: 'Smell a rat' means to sense that something is dishonest or wrong, without yet having proof. "The moment they asked for payment upfront, I smelled a rat."
quests.origin: Possibly from the behavior of cats or dogs detecting a hidden rat by scent before it's visible, extended figuratively to sensing hidden deception.

quests.instruction: The numbers in the financial report didn't match the bank statements at all, and the accountant immediately felt that ___ was going on.
quests.hint: It's a casual way of saying something seems suspicious or dishonest.
quests.explanation: 'Something's fishy' means a situation seems suspicious or dishonest. "His explanation for the missing funds sounded fishy."
quests.origin: Possibly linked to the strong, often off-putting smell of fish gone bad, used as a metaphor for suspicion.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: So impressively appealing that it raises suspicion the claim must be false or exaggerated.
quests.explanation: 'Too good to be true' describes something so appealing it raises suspicion of being false. "A luxury apartment at that price sounded too good to be true."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase expressing the intuitive rule that unusually generous claims often hide a catch.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The new regional manager, barely a month into the role, started overriding decisions from every department just to demonstrate his authority."
quests.hint: It's about using your position or authority in a heavy-handed, often unwelcome way.
quests.explanation: 'Throw your weight around' means to use your authority in a heavy-handed, often unwelcome way. "He's been throwing his weight around ever since the promotion."
quests.origin: A literal image of using physical bulk to push others aside, applied figuratively to using status to dominate a situation.

quests.instruction: Instead of discussing the schedule change like everyone else, the senior partner simply ___ and declared the decision final.
quests.hint: It means using your official position or seniority to override someone, rather than persuading them.
quests.explanation: 'Pull rank' means to use your official position or seniority to get your way. "She pulled rank and overruled the whole team's decision."
quests.origin: A military metaphor, describing a superior officer invoking their formal rank to command obedience from subordinates.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Behave in a superior, condescending way toward someone because of an advantage you have over them.
quests.explanation: 'Lord it over someone' means to behave arrogantly superior toward them because of some advantage. "Ever since he got promoted, he's lorded it over his former peers."
quests.origin: Uses 'lord' as a verb, evoking the condescending authority historically associated with feudal lords over their subjects.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "She marched straight up to her neighbor's door, clearly ready to confront him about the loud music every night that week."
quests.hint: It's about having a specific grievance you intend to raise directly with someone.
quests.explanation: 'Have a bone to pick' means to have a specific grievance you intend to address with someone. "I've got a bone to pick with you about that email you sent."
quests.origin: A literal image of two dogs fighting over a single bone, extended figuratively to an unresolved dispute needing to be settled.

quests.instruction: Knowing exactly how insecure he was about his lack of a degree, she brought it up during the argument specifically to ___.
quests.hint: It means to target someone's most sensitive vulnerability, deliberately causing maximum emotional pain.
quests.explanation: 'Hit where it hurts' means to target someone's most sensitive vulnerability deliberately. "His comment about her failed business really hit where it hurts."
quests.origin: A literal, physical metaphor for striking at the most painful, sensitive point, applied figuratively to emotional attacks.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Deliberately make an already painful situation even more painful, often cruelly.
quests.explanation: 'Twist the knife' means to deliberately worsen an already painful situation. "Bringing up his ex at the party was just twisting the knife."
quests.origin: A vivid, violent image of a knife already causing injury being deliberately twisted to increase the pain further.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The reporter's sudden, unexpected question about the scandal completely surprised the spokesperson, who stumbled over his prepared answers."
quests.hint: It's about surprising someone when they weren't prepared or expecting it.
quests.explanation: 'Catch someone off guard' means to surprise them when they weren't prepared. "The sudden question about layoffs caught the CEO off guard."
quests.origin: A literal boxing and fencing image: a fighter 'off guard' has lowered their defenses and is vulnerable to a surprise attack.

quests.instruction: The security footage showed him taking cash directly from the register, leaving no doubt — he was completely ___.
quests.hint: It's about being discovered in the middle of clearly doing something wrong, with undeniable proof.
quests.explanation: 'Caught red-handed' means being discovered in the act of doing something wrong, with clear proof. "He was caught red-handed copying answers during the exam."
quests.origin: From old Scottish law, referring to a person literally caught with blood on their hands right after committing a violent crime.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Completely surprised by something negative that you had no warning was coming.
quests.explanation: 'Blindsided' means completely surprised by an unexpected, usually negative, event. "She was blindsided by the sudden breakup — she'd had no idea anything was wrong."
quests.origin: A literal image from American football, where a player is hit hard from their blind side, unable to see the impact coming.

quests.word: BURY YOUR HEAD IN THE SAND
quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Even as the company's losses grew every month, the founder refused to look at the financial reports or discuss the possibility of shutting down."
quests.hint: It's about deliberately ignoring a serious problem instead of confronting it, often out of denial.
options: BURY YOUR HEAD IN THE SAND
quests.explanation: 'Bury your head in the sand' means to deliberately ignore a serious problem instead of dealing with it. "Ignoring the warning signs is just burying your head in the sand."
quests.correctAnswer: BURY YOUR HEAD IN THE SAND
quests.origin: Based on a popular but factually inaccurate belief that ostriches bury their heads in sand when frightened — a myth that nonetheless produced a lasting idiom.

quests.instruction: The manager knew about the safety violations on the factory floor but chose to ___ rather than deal with the paperwork and cost of fixing them.
quests.hint: It means deliberately choosing not to notice or address a known wrongdoing.
options: BURY YOUR HEAD IN THE SAND
quests.explanation: 'Look the other way' means to deliberately avoid noticing or addressing known wrongdoing. "Security looked the other way when the regulars snuck in drinks."
quests.origin: A literal image of physically turning your gaze away from something happening in front of you, avoiding direct acknowledgment.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Deliberately ignore something wrong that you're fully aware is happening.
options: BURY YOUR HEAD IN THE SAND
quests.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye' means to deliberately overlook a problem or wrongdoing you know about. "The landlord turned a blind eye to the unauthorized subletting."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'turn a blind eye' — traditionally linked to a disputed story about Admiral Nelson at the Battle of Copenhagen.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The moment the manager noticed two employees starting to gossip about a coworker, she pulled them aside immediately before it could spread any further."
quests.hint: It's about stopping a problem at its very earliest stage, before it can grow into something bigger.
quests.explanation: 'Nip it in the bud' means to stop a problem at its earliest stage before it grows worse. "The teacher nipped the disruptive behavior in the bud right away."
quests.origin: A literal gardening image of pinching off a plant's bud before it can bloom, preventing further unwanted growth.

quests.instruction: As the only experienced person on the team, she spent most days jumping from one urgent crisis to another, rarely getting to any planned, proactive work at all.
quests.hint: It means constantly reacting to urgent problems as they arise, rather than working proactively.
quests.explanation: 'Put out fires' means to spend your time reacting to urgent problems rather than working proactively. "As team lead, half my week is just putting out fires."
quests.origin: A literal firefighting image extended to any constant, reactive crisis management in a workplace or personal life.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Prevent something unwanted from getting worse or advancing further, at least temporarily.
quests.explanation: 'Keep something at bay' means to prevent it from advancing or worsening, at least for now. "Regular maintenance keeps bigger repair costs at bay."
quests.origin: From hunting, where a cornered animal 'held at bay' is kept at a safe distance, unable to advance further.
